But it is still possible that the mostly popular Democratic governor of the largest Democratic party stronghold in the country could lose . And if that happens , the person most likely to replace him is a Trump-supporting talk radio host supported by fewer than 30 per cent of Californians . <p> What the heck ? <p> Here 's what you need to know to get caught up on Tuesday 's recall election . <p> What 's going on ? <p> Newsom was elected governor in 2018 with 62 per cent of the vote in a state that is among the most reliably Democratic-voting in the U.S. . The next regularly scheduled election for governor is in November 2022 . <p> Despite some controversy over Newsom 's handling of the COVID-19 epidemic ( including @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in violation of his own pandemic guidelines ) , there is n't any major scandal driving the campaign to remove him from office . In fact , polls suggest that he remains relatively popular , with an approval rating that has hovered above 50 per cent all year . ( By way of comparison , Biden 's current approval rating is 45 per cent . ) <p> Still , those who want him removed from office managed to get enough signatures on a petition to trigger the recall election that takes place Tuesday . <p> Huh ? If Newsom is popular , why is there a recall election ? <p> California 's political system allows voters to pass specific propositions that tie the hands of their elected officials -- writer Michael Lewis once described it as " designed mainly to maximize the likelihood that voters will continue to despise the people they elect . " <p> California residents have the easiest process of any state to try to turf those politicians whom they despise . While some states require a felony conviction or serious misconduct , California does not require @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that triggers a recall vote to be signed by 25 per cent of the number of voters in the previous election ; California 's threshold of just 12 per cent is the lowest in the country . <p> There have been 55 attempts to remove California 's governor since the state 's recall law was enacted in 1913 . The only one that actually led to a vote was in 2003 , when Democrat Gray Davis was removed and replaced by Republican Arnold Schwarzenegger . <p> So how does it work ? <p> The vote is mostly being conducted by mail , although a sizable percentage may drop off their ballots in person on Tuesday . Each ballot contains two questions : should Newsom be recalled , and who should replace him . <p> If Newsom receives 50 per cent support on the first question , the recall will have been defeated and the second question will become irrelevant . However , if a majority votes to remove Newsom , then the winner of the most votes on the second question -- no matter how small a percentage that person @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ anyone from running against Newsom , fearing that an attractive alternative might split their base , so most of the 49 candidates to replace him are Republicans or fringey independents . With so many candidates , it 's possible that a replacement governor could win with less than three per cent of the vote . And although such an extreme scenario is unlikely , it is very likely that the winner in a recall scenario would take office with much less than a majority of the vote , and with fewer votes than were cast to keep Newsom in office . <p> However , as the poll crunching experts point out , it 's very hard to know what to expect on election day . It 's not a regularly scheduled election year , so turnout is hard to predict . It 's a mostly Democratic state with a moderately popular incumbent , which would seem to favour Newsom . But " throw the bums out " is often a more motivating ballot prompt than " the status quo is mostly fine . " <p> If Newsom is recalled , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Larry Elder , a Los Angeles talk show host who would repeal COVID-19 mask and vaccination mandates , opposes legal abortion , has called climate change a " crock " and wants to eliminate the minimum wage . <p> The somewhat Trumpy Elder has accomplished the interesting feat of being opposed by a two-thirds majority of poll respondents , while simultaneously lapping the pack of alternatives . With 28 per cent support , according to the fivethirtyeight.com poll average , he is n't exactly popular . But the next highest name on the ballot is real estate YouTuber Kevin Paffrath ( the lone registered Democrat ) with only seven per cent support , followed by former San Diego mayor Kevin Faulconer at five per cent . @@53189296 <h> Share this article <p> Share this article <p> OTTAWA , ON , Sept. 29 , 2021 /CNW Telbec/ - A new report from the Canadian Institute for Climate Choices , Canada 's independent climate policy research institute , finds that climate change impacts could leave Canadians physically and financially under water as a warming and increasingly volatile climate damages public and private infrastructure . Homes , buildings and critical infrastructure are all at risk , unless new investment and improved regulation make these assets more resilient to the changing climate . <p> Under Water : The Costs of Climate Change for Canada 's Infrastructure is the largest study to date of these kinds of impacts . It focuses on three types of climate change impacts to some of Canada 's most vital infrastructure : flooding of homes and buildings , damage to roads and rails , and impacts on Canada 's electricity grids . Findings include : <p> Flood damage to homes and buildings could increase fivefold by mid-century and tenfold by end of century , with costs as high as $13.6B annually . <p> Damage to roads and railways could increase by up to $5.4B annually by @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of century . <p> Costs to repair and maintain electrical infrastructure could more than double by mid-century and triple by end of century , costing up to $4.1B annually . <p> The Institute 's report concludes with specific recommendations for governments to direct public and private investment toward more resilient infrastructure -- changes that will save the country billions of dollars in reduced loss and damage . <p> Among the cost savings of proactive investment identified : <p> Shoreline protection and moving homes out of high-risk areas can reduce the future costs of coastal flooding by up to 90 per cent . <p> Repaving roads with resilient materials can reduce costs by over 90 per cent . <p> Using resilient materials when updating electrical infrastructure can reduce damage costs by 80 per cent . <p> QUOTES <p> " Climate change is a massive threat to the public and private infrastructure that underpins Canada 's prosperity . The challenge for governments today is to rapidly shift how infrastructure decisions are made in ways that factor in a changing climate . @@53189316 <p> Canada 's infrastructure is already vulnerable to a changing climate and the problem will get worse if all levels of government do n't get more serious about the challenge ahead , a new report warns . <p> The report from the Canadian Institute for Climate Choices ( CICC ) , an independent think tank , shows that without " new investment and improved regulation , " Canada 's infrastructure wo n't be able to withstand the effects of climate change , which could leave " Canadians physically and financially under water , " the report says . <p> " Because decisions around infrastructure in Canada right now are n't accounting for a warming climate , we 're potentially going to be on the hook for billions of dollars in costs within even just a couple of decades , " said Ryan Ness , a research director at the CICC , in an interview with iPolitics on Tuesday . <p> " On the flip side , we have opportunities to dramatically minimize those costs by investing proactively in adaptation , by building infrastructure that 's more robust , by not building it in places that are risky , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it more resilient to a more volatile climate , " he continued . <p> The report highlights three key areas where Canada 's infrastructure falls short and where more investment and regulation is urgently needed : flooding of homes and buildings , damage to roads and rails , and effects on Canada 's electricity grids . <p> Inland flooding currently costs Canadians about $1.3 billion annually , the report says , but could increase to nearly $7 billion by midcentury , and nearly $10 billion by the end of the century if Canada does n't succeed in reducing emissions . <p> Reducing emissions reduces the likelihood of more precipitation and higher water levels , of the century . <p> Coastal flooding does n't cost nearly as much , largely because there are fewer people and buildings on Canada 's coasts . <p> By the end of the century , damages @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ end of the century . <p> Climate-related rail maintenance and repair costs considerably less than roads , though the big risks comes from climate-related delays . The report estimates climate-related delays could cost as much as $2 billion annually . <p> The risk to Canada 's electricity system also comes in two forms : direct costs from maintenance and repair , and slowing the energy transition to net zero . <p> The damage includes hotter air reducing power transformers ' lifespan and transmission capacity , and speeding the decay of the wood poles transformers sit on . <p> The projected annual cost for climate-related damages to electricity transmission and distribution infrastructure at the beginning of the current century was about $1.3 billion , the report says . <p> In a low-emission scenario , that could rise to just under $1.8 billion , whereas in a high-emission scenario it could rise to over $3.5 billion , annually . <p> Proactive adaptation can dramatically reduce the potential costs of having infrastructure not suited to a changing climate -- by anywhere from 50 to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ order to effectively adapt to the changing climate and the risks to Canada 's infrastructure , the report makes four recommendations . <p> Canada 's flood mapping regime does n't fully account for all the at-risk areas , allowing new buildings to go in flood-prone areas , the report says . The lack of information on flood patterns also severely hampers any adaptation measures . <p> " If public and private infrastructure owners are not made aware of and accountable for climate risk , they will continue to accumulate risk that will grow dramatically with climate change , " the report says . <p> Third , climate resilience and adaptation needs to be taken into account for all infrastructure spending and regulatory decisions . <p> Because infrastructure tends to last a long time , " decisions made today -- and yesterday -- will dictate the resilience of Canada 's infrastructure to climate change over the remainder of the century , " the report says . <p> Fourth , safety nets need to be created for those most vulnerable to climate change . <p> " Homeowners who are already struggling to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ have even less money to spend if banks raise mortgage rates and insurers raise property insurance premiums in flood-prone areas . @@53190051 <h> You are here <p> rabble blogs are the personal pages of some of Canada 's most insightful progressive activists and commentators . All opinions belong to the writer ; however , writers are expected to adhere to our guidelines . We welcome new bloggers -- contact us for details . <h> Changing our animals ' food could solve big problems <p> The environmental implications of feeding eight billion people are enormous . That 's also true for keeping the ever-increasing population of domesticated animals fed , whether pets or livestock . <p> Just as there are better ways to feed people , there are better ways to feed animals . In some cases , it would be best not to raise or keep the animals at all , but for others , simple solutions could substantially reduce environmental damage . <p> With farmed animals , including fish , it 's about the ways we feed ourselves and the animals we eat . Extensive research shows that raising animals for meat , especially cows and sheep , creates massive environmental problems , from nitrogen runoff into waterways to greenhouse gas emissions , including methane . <p> A 2019 Lancet @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and with fewer animal source foods confers both improved health and environmental benefits . " It found switching to more plant-based diets and improving food production practices would help reduce negative impacts related to climate change , land system change , freshwater use , nitrogen and phosphorous cycling and biodiversity loss . <p> In the short term , we should strive to reduce some impacts of raising animals for food . One solution is changing their feed . Methane from livestock manure and " gastroenteric releases " ( burps and farts ) makes up about 32 per cent of human-caused methane emissions . Although methane remains in the atmosphere for a shorter time than carbon dioxide , it 's a deadly pollutant and , over 20 years , up to 80 times more potent as a greenhouse gas . <p> Researchers are exploring feeds made from or supplemented with everything from seaweed or algae to canola to reduce flatulence in cattle , and at ways to better treat , or even use , manure , such as covering or composting it , or using it to produce biogas . By @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ steers , University of California Davis researchers cut methane emissions by 80 per cent . However , critics point out this does n't address the far greater volume of emissions from pastured cattle . <p> Feed is also one area to help resolve a major environmental impact of companion and service animals . Cats and dogs , especially , consume a lot of meat . The estimated 8.2 million pet dogs and 8.3 million cats in Canada and 80 million dogs and 60 million cats in the U.S. often eat relatively high-quality meat products , so the impacts are substantial . <p> One study found " cats and dogs account for 25 to 30 per cent of the environmental impact of meat consumption in the United States , and are responsible for creating approximately 64 million tons of carbon dioxide each year . " They also produce millions of tonnes of poop every year , much of it individually wrapped before being sent to landfill , and some contaminating waterways with bacteria , viruses and parasites . <p> Finding a good source of protein and other essential nutrients with fewer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ big ones like Nestl ? -owned Purina , are marketing pet foods made with insect protein . An Ontario company , Hope , is using a mix of black soldier fly protein , chickpeas , yeast and algae . <p> I once suggested it would be better to feed farmed salmon insects than other fish . Brad Marchant heard , and founded Enterra ( which I invested in ) . It uses black soldier fly larvae for fish and other animal feed . The larvae are rich in protein , calcium , phosphorous , iron and zinc and are easy to raise . Combining them with the other ingredients results in a pet food that 's healthier overall than meat-based products , with far fewer environmental impacts -- and it has spinoff benefits , such as diverting waste to feed the insects . <p> A 2017 Dutch review found insect farming requires much less land and water than livestock , has lower greenhouse gas emissions and high feed conversion efficiencies , and is useful as animal or aqua feed . A U.S. company claims " an acre of land can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pounds of poultry , " but can yield " 65,000 pounds of cricket or 130,000 pounds of black soldier fly larvae . " <p> Insects are also a healthy protein source for people around the world and may gradually gain greater acceptance here . <p> The interrelated climate and biodiversity crises are at a point where many solutions are needed . Changing how we feed the animals we keep can make a difference . It might even make our animal companions healthier . <p> David Suzuki is a scientist , broadcaster , author and co-founder of the David Suzuki Foundation . These are policies that you are seeing other climate-leading jurisdictions do . I personally feel like Canada is in a good position going into COP 26 . <p> Petrevan : Depends on the day . Some days , I feel tremendously optimistic about what leaders in the world are doing ; countries , particularly in Europe , and even in the U.K. , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ policy that is going to have to be put in place , not only to reduce emissions , but also to help the global economy through the transition . And then other days , I look at how woefully inadequate the funding is for third-world countries to help them adopt climate-change ambition . I look at China , and I say , yes , you 're stopping funding coal abroad , but yet you 're still scaling it up domestically , and I feel less optimistic . I think it 's true for anybody who works in this area of policy that it really is a wave of up and down .

The government is even doubling down , claiming we have to expand fossil carbon extraction because @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ emissions cutting . ... <p> Curious whether any country has been able to pull off this seemingly counter-intuitive combo of extracting more while emitting less , I went digging through the data for Canada and several of its peer nations . What I found is the opposite . Nations that ramped down their fossil fuel extraction were the ones that cut their emissions , while nations that increased extraction failed . To illustrate this consistent link between extraction and emissions , I 've created a series of charts showing what Canada and a group of its peers have done . ... <p> The nations I chose to research are the Group of Seven ( G7 ) nations : Canada , France , Germany , Italy , Japan , the United Kingdom , the United States , and the European Union . With just one-sixth of the world population , they hold more than half the world 's wealth , produce half the global GDP , and emit a third of global climate pollution . ... I also included two other peer nations that , like Canada , have significantly increased @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and Norway ( Europe 's biggest oil producer ) . ... <p> My first chart shows how emissions and extraction have changed since 1990 for all these nations . That year , 1990 , is the international baseline year for comparing climate progress between nations . <p> National emissions changes are shown as solid bars , while the changes in fossil carbon extraction are shown by the paler , dashed-line bars tucked behind them . Green is reductions ; red is increases . <p> For example , Canada 's solid red bar shows our emissions increased 21 per cent since 1990 . That 's 10 times worse than the Americans , whose emissions rose two per cent over these years . And Canada 's red dashed-line bar shows that along the way , we 've increased fossil carbon extraction by an off-the-chart 100 per cent . Up and up ; red and red . <p> The most obvious pattern that jumps out at me in this chart -- only nations that reduced fossil carbon extraction , cut emissions . These are the double green bars . Clearly , wealthy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it while reducing fossil fuel extraction . <p> The chart 's red bars show the opposite is true . No nation that increased fossil carbon extraction cut emissions . Like Canada , they all promised repeatedly to cut emissions . Only Australia among developed nations has done worse , and only by a small margin as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ next look more closely at extraction trends in individual nations . ... <p> Back in 1990 , Germany was extracting the most in this group . In fact , it was the world 's third-biggest coal producer -- digging up nearly 900 million tonnes of CO2 ( MtCO2 ) worth of coal alone each year . <p> Since then , both the Germans and British significantly reduced their fossil carbon extraction to less than 300 MtCO2 worth per year . As we saw above , all the nations that cutextraction also cut emissions . Sure enough , as extraction fell , Germany 's emissions fell 35 per cent and the U.K. 's by 43 per cent . As an additional benefit , these nations have much less work remaining to transition their fossil fuel workers and sector to net-zero . <p> Canada and Australia took the opposite path . Both doubled the fossil carbon extracted each year . Canada now extracts four times more than the Germans or British do -- 1,300 MtCO2 worth per year . <p> Our relentless increase in fossil carbon extraction has pushed Canadian fossil fuel @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ gas economic sector ever higher up the net-zero carbon cliff . Entitled Let 's talk @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in order to gauge how the community feels about the issue . It can also be accessed at the website above . <p> " This is an important engagement activity with the public , " said Future Climate Leaders project co-ordinator Lee Theodore . " It 's not very often that we get to poll information from the public versus putting information to the public . <p> " These kid submissions will be great , but it 's just a way to remind people that climate change is a part of the conversation and we hope that people can have them locally , together . " <p> The River Institute 's mandate is n't solely to protect the river -- it also strives to protect the ecosystems surrounding it . It therefore wants to help promote information around climate change . That 's why it launched Future Climate Leaders , a project whose goal is to increase public awareness about climate change within society 's different levels . <h> Advertisement <p> Story continues below <p> This advertisement has not loaded yet , but your article continues below . <h> Article @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a very vocal file , but it is still a concern all the same , " said Theodore . " Everybody understands climate change at their own level . I 've talked with proponents and people that would probably be seemingly against the idea of climate change and across the board , there is an understanding that there is an impact in their lives in on way , shape or form . <p> " People are having conversations -- they are aware . " <p> Theodore , through the survey , hopes to receive feedback from at least 1,000 residents . It 's an ambitious goal , but he 's confident it can happen . There are also plans to survey neighbouring communities as well in order to get data from area residents as well . That would enable the creation of a large data pool , which could then be used for decision-making in Ottawa . <p> That same data will then be stored by the city and will be used to not only to create a baseline of understanding of what the community is thinking , believing and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it in taking informed decisions . <p> So far , about a dozen submissions for the youths challenge have been received . The initiative has been pitched to three local schools , one of which has accepted it . It 's expected that the two other ones will also come on board . <p> " It 's new and we 'll see what the uptick becomes and also , it is not to say that we can not bring this back again as another campaign in the future really quickly , " said Theodore . " Climate change is going to take the resolve of every capable human being possible . The challenge is , how is Cornwall , Ontario , impacting Edmonton Alberta , or Glasgow Scotland ? The trick to all of this is lifestyle change and that can happen locally at home . " <p> Future Climate Leaders is also currently working on launching its own website in the near future . For now , anyone wanting to keep up with the initiative can do so on the Future Climate Leaders ' Facebook page . <h> Share @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <h> Advertisement <p> Story continues below <p> This advertisement has not loaded yet , but your article continues below . <h> News Near Cornwall <h> This Week in Flyers <h> Comments <p> Postmedia is committed to maintaining a lively but civil forum for discussion and encourage all readers to share their views on our articles . @@53194156 <p> Park Drive , which loops through Vancouver 's Stanley Park , was converted into a one- and two-lane bicycle route throughout the COVID-19 pandemic.City of Vancouver <p> A B.C. Supreme Court has denied a judicial review brought forward by a group of Stanley Park restaurateurs who challenged the City of Vancouver for its decision to convert a major park thoroughfare into a dedicated bike lane . <p> The judgment , handed down earlier this week , pitted the owners of the Teahouse , Stanley Park Pavilion and Prospect Point Bar and Grill against the Vancouver Board of Parks and Recreation . <p> The group of restaurateurs had applied for a judicial review of a park board resolution to convert Park Drive , which circumnavigates Stanley Park , into a bicycle route . <p> The restaurateurs argued that designating the route a permanent bike lane to reduce carbon emissions and appease a public opinion survey was carried out using " clear logical fallacies , such as circular reasoning , false dilemmas , unfounded generalizations or an absurd premise . " <h> PANDEMIC RESPONSE TO AN EVOLVING CITY <p> In her decision , Justice Sheila Tucker reviewed the evolution of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 10 park board decision . <p> Starting in January 2019 , the city declared a climate emergency and passed a number of resolutions to reduce emissions . City council would soon approve " big moves " to cut carbon emissions by transitioning away from gas-powered vehicles and moving toward a 2030 goal where two-thirds of all trips in the city were taken by foot , bicycle or transit . <p> Then coronavirus hit . On March 11 , the World Health Organization declared the spread of COVID-19 a pandemic , and within a week , B.C. 's provincial health officer followed suit . <p> The park board responded by opening up the city in places where it could help people physical distance . On April 8 , it barred vehicle traffic from Park Drive and converted it into a cycling path separate from the Stanley Park Seawall . <p> By early summer , the park board launched a study to look at reducing car traffic inside Stanley Park on a permanent basis . In the motion , the park board said it had received comments from the public that fewer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Turning the eastbound lane along Beach Avenue over to cyclists and pedestrians reduced traffic and access to Stanley Park even more , noted the motion . <p> A year later , the park board reopened one lane of traffic to motor vehicles , with the other remaining a cycling path . Meanwhile , a Stanley Park mobility study was underway , gauging public opinion on the one- and two-lane cycling paths . <p> Of the nearly 11,000 respondents , 66 per cent said they wanted some of the road reserved for cyclists . A further 71 per cent said their experience was either better or no different with both lanes turned over to cyclists , and 51 per cent said the same about the one-lane cyclist regime . Only 36 per cent said they wanted Park Drive to remain a right-of-way for motor vehicle traffic . <p> At one stage in the process , the park board received over 750 letters -- including from the restaurateurs -- ranging from passionately for and vehemently against the proposal to limit Park Drive to bike traffic . <p> In submissions to the court @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ saying it was not a representative sample . <h> REDUCING EMISSIONS , PUBLIC SURVEY ' NOT REASONABLE ' <p> Incorporated under Ferguson Point Restaurants Inc. and Stanley Park Operations Ltd. , the restaurant owners argued the park board went ahead with the bike lane based on the city 's need to reduce carbon emissions and the Stanley Park public survey results . Neither , said the petitioners , were reasonable bases for the decision . <p> The park board , they added , acted under an " almost certainly false " assumption the bike lane would reduce carbon emissions . In fact , they told the court , the bike lane would lead to more congestion and idling of vehicles along Park Drive , while other park users would increase emissions by driving further to car-accessible parks . <p> They also alleged that it was unreasonable to rely on the public survey results as they were flawed and inadequate . The owners said the park board failed to consider the negative effects on the bike lane , such as reduced access for people with mobility problems , small children and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ other parks ; and impacts on park businesses , such as their own . <p> But the judge found the restaurateurs ' argument was an oversimplification : reducing carbon emissions and considering the results of a public survey merely " set the scene for the debate " that weighed a number of factors , from the impact of gas- and diesel-vehicle emissions on climate change to encouraging cycling for health and safety reasons . <p> " The resolution is a small and exploratory component in a wide-ranging policy response to a social dilemma , not an operational solution to emission volumes , " wrote Tucker . <p> She added : " A decision need not be flawless in order to be reasonable . "

@@53194521 <p> The provincial government should spend $1 million annually reviewing the Okanagan Lake drainage system with a view to eventually replacing the 60-year-old dam at Penticton , provincial finance officials were told Wednesday . <p> The provincial government should spend $1 million annually reviewing the Okanagan Lake drainage system with a view to eventually replacing the 60-year-old dam at Penticton , provincial finance officials were told Wednesday . <p> The Okanagan dam at Penticton is 60 years old and needs to be replaced to better cope with the realities of climate change , water managers say . <p> A structure like the dam - which controls the outflow of water from Okanagan Lake to lakes further south in the Valley - typically lasts 70-80 years , the Okanagan Basin Water Board says . <p> Not only is the dam nearing the end of its operational lifespan , its current design is inadequate to rapidly and effectively respond to lake levels that can change quickly , the OBWB says . <p> " It is inadequate for managing future floods in its current state , given the increased volume and frequency of floods as a result of climate change , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " OBWM executive director Anna Warwick Sears told provincial finance officials during a 2022 budget consultation meeting on Wednesday . <p> The OBWB hopes the government will allocate $1 million annually for the next five years for a comprehensive review of the Okanagan Lake drainage system . The work would identify flaws in the current operation , and suggest what kind of improvements or new infrastructure are better needed to manage the seasonal elevation changes in Okanagan Lake . <p> In her budget submission , Warwick Sears also asked the government to restore funding for a program that inspects vessels being towed into B.C. for invasive quagga and zebra mussels . <p> Government provided $3.8 million for the inspection stations in 2017 , but the amount has been reduced since then . <p> The mussels , if they become established in B.C. , will foul swimming beaches , clog water infrastructure , and negatively affect aquatic ecosystems , the OBWB says .

@@53195015 <h> You are here <h> New MPs : your reading list starts here <p> While voting is important , the mobilization that occurs between elections is actually just as important . <p> The Liberal Party has formed another minority government , perhaps giving the federal NDP new energy as it tries to leverage the power and strategy of its 25 elected Members . What is absolutely clear when assessing the percentage of the popular vote garnered by each party is the drastic need for electoral reform lest the voting public become even more cynical in future ( voter turnout was at a mere 59 per cent in this election -- a historic low ) . That issue did n't even make headlines in this election . <p> Throughout the past several weeks of electioneering , I did not hear the words agriculture or farmer or family farm come through on the national stage via debates , campaign releases , or other newsers . <p> Meanwhile , each party did include platform commitments related to agriculture . The election is over you say ! True -- but those commitments are on paper and should be used to remind elected Members @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Some organizations have provided summaries . This campaign " promise " round-up from the National Farmers Union could come in handy in future for those advocating on issues related to the future of family farms , food security and sovereignty , and related climate change issues . <p> One of the issues that has gained momentum in 2021 , in part due to the income fragility of this ongoing pandemic , is a guaranteed annual income -- also known as a guaranteed livable basic income . A commitment to this pillar was clear in the NDP platform but not mentioned at all in the Liberal platform . <p> A basic annual income has a very clear connection to food production in this country and without one , we are jeopardizing our ability to support local , sustainable , food systems . <p> A recent report published by Ontario Region 3 of the National Farmers ' Union makes the important link between the need for farm labour and a basic livable income . <p> Reframing the Farm Labour Crisis is based on a survey of more than 700 Ontario farmers @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a livable wage for farm labour on family and smaller farms . This detailed report covers temporary farm labour , local farm labour , training and support for those interested in working on family farms and programs to support those interested in producing food more generally . <p> Again , the pandemic has shown just how fragile our homegrown food production systems are . Included in the report is a call for basic income to ensure a fair wage for farm labour and also explains why family farm labourers need such a basic income guarantee -- as well as access to Employment Insurance and universal paid sick days -- to allow them a sustainable livelihood from farm work . It is a report filled with substantial issues . <p> A summary which leads into the report 's recommendations states : <p> " Ontario 's small to mid-sized farms are robust agricultural job creators . In fact , the Farm Labour Project found that farms under 70 acres were more likely to be employing Ontarians than their larger counterparts . These modest farms are also the knowledge incubators for the next @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , training , and retention practices will be vital to resolving the skilled-labour shortage in the agricultural sector . Similarly , creating viable conduits to farm ownership for seasoned farm workers through land-linking , land-sharing and/or co-operative opportunities will be crucial to offset soaring land prices and ensure there are successors for our aging population of farm operators . However , without living wages/incomes we are unlikely to attract enough Ontarians willing to acquire the skills and dedicate their lives to agricultural production . " <p> Interestingly the report also includes a recommendation on the creation of co-operatives : <p> Support Co-operative Initiatives : Less than 5% of farms surveyed were co-operatives , but almost 13% would consider forming a cooperative . Over 48% of workers were interested in co-operative farming opportunities . Given the financial constraints on farm operators and staff , it is recommended that farm organizations work closely with Local Food and Farm Co-ops ( LFFC ) to support farmers wishing to start or transition to co-operative models . <p> So now -- as the newly elected Members of Parliament are trying to find their seats and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ should be digging into . We need many MPs thinking about food production and post-pandemic models or programs -- not just those responsible for the agriculture file . Farming and food production encompasses many issues related to various aspects of our lives , from seed , pesticides , land use , labour and young workers , training , climate change and yes , even co-operatives . <p> These are links that need to be strengthened post-voting day . Food sovereignty through local agriculture is a good place to start . <p> Supporting and encouraging co-operatives in any sector , including agriculture , can help to create stability , loyalty , employment and a workable alternative to succession planning . Indeed , climate policies and pledges flowed left and right leading up to the federal election . However , largely absent from the mainstream dialogue on the shifting energy landscape is any pragmatic talk about the productive use of carbon emissions . <p> That 's right -- rather than just reducing , we can use carbon emissions as a building block for other industrial processes and products . On the surface , it 's rather simple : by taking more of the carbon from these processes and using it as a feedstock , we decrease the amount released into the atmosphere . <p> Take , for example , the chemical industry . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fuel production , there is enormous benefit to be had from the capture and use of carbon to make sustainable , value-added synthetic fuels to replace some of the need to refine hydrocarbons from underground . By making liquid fuels that can replace diesel and gasoline , we are substituting a carbon-neutral process for a carbon-intensive one . Although this only locks in carbon until the synthetic fuel is combusted , it ultimately reduces net emissions . <p> And there are more ways to use CO2 . Take , for example , everyday products that act as storage , with emissions captured from the air and then processed into a powder before being incorporated into things like yoga mats , crayons and planters . Perhaps a more well-known example is concrete -- essential for construction , a centrepiece for making housing more affordable -- which uses emissions in numerous different ways , with opportunities for larger-scale deployment . There are Canadian companies already using and growing these kinds of technologies that could keep carbon out of the atmosphere for a century or more . <p> Essentially , rather than exacerbating @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> This is all part of the emerging concept of a circular economy -- one based on eliminating waste and pollution , the circulation of products and materials , and the regeneration of nature . In contrast , the linear economy that has dominated the global industrial systems since the Industrial Revolution sees carbon extracted , produced , distributed , and consumed before being discarded -- both as solid waste and in the form of gaseous emissions . <p> Of course , historically , entrepreneurs have generally sought ways to make productive use of byproducts . In fact , gasoline itself was once considered a waste byproduct and discarded . <p> Canada is already considered a global leader in carbon capture , and there is immense potential in the processing of industrial emissions into sustainable , value-added biofuels and products . Alternative uses for carbon need to be a bigger part of the discussion . Our need for carbon can be balanced with climate protection , innovation , and resource conservation . Ultimately , we need to take a more nuanced view of how to reduce GHGs in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ products is a pragmatic approach Canadians should be aware of . <p> Krystle Wittevrongel is a public policy analyst at the Montreal Economic Institute . @@53197312 <p> Canadians are overjoyed at the two Michaels ' release from imprisonment in China , and relieved that Canada 's relations with the country might return to normal . <p> While China 's use of Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou in hostage diplomacy was loathsome and rightfully condemned , the Michaels ' release is but a small step on a long road to more normal relations , which must involve China 's treaty compliance under international law . <p> Over the past five years or so , China has ignored its obligations under multiple international treaties to which it 's a party . <p> Examples include : the Law of the Sea Convention , which China ignored by rejecting the 2016 arbitral ruling in the South China Sea ; the Convention against Racial Discrimination that China has disregarded by abusing Uighur people in Xinjiang ; the Sino-British Declaration that China dismissed by suppressing civil and legal rights in Hong Kong ; and the World Trade Organization agreement , whose rule-of-law and market-economy requirements China has openly flouted . <p> China 's detention of the two Michaels involved particularly egregious violations of the bilateral consular treaty with Canada , as well @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and their treatment while in custody . <p> The People 's Republic of China ( PRC ) government is fond of proclaiming that its conduct in these matters has been according to law . However , a strong and widespread consensus among international specialist observers concludes that law in the PRC is not a meaningful constraint on the Party-state but rather is simply an instrument of its rule . <p> The disparities between China 's treatment of the Two Michaels and Canada 's treatment of Meng underscored the difference between China 's socialist legal system and the rule of law in Canada -- attested to by none other than Meng herself in thanking the Canadian Department of Justice for its " steadfast adherence to the rule of law . " Moreover , China 's repeated claims that its sovereignty overrules its treaty obligations contradict the basic principles of international law that treaties are by definition a diminution of sovereignty accepted voluntarily by member states . Treaty compliance expresses member states ' commitment to the international rule of law . <p> As a middle power , Canada depends on the rule-based @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ matters of human rights , trade and investment , climate change , or global public health , Canada needs the international rules-based order . <p> As the second-largest economy in the world , with growing military power and political influence , China 's commitment to fulfilling its treaty obligations is essential . China is now applying to join the Comprehensive and Progressive Trans Pacific Partnership ( CPTPP ) and one can only wonder whether it will repeat its record of performance under the WTO -- a question made all the more fraught by Beijing 's opposition to Taiwan 's joining CPTPP even though Taiwan 's economy meets the standards for entry more fully than China 's does . <p> Rebuilding Canada-China relations requires that China renew its commitment to international law and treaty compliance . <p> Canada can take several steps to achieve this goal with regard to bilateral and multilateral treaties : <p> Incorporate into future treaties with China side-agreements by which China commits to fulsome and good-faith compliance in accordance with international law . <p> For existing treaties , Canada and China can exchange interpretive notes reaffirming their @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Work with the UN International Law Commission to expand existing work on the UN 's " Programme of Action to Strengthen the Rule of Law at the National and International Levels " to include clarification that treaty member states may not justify failure to uphold treaty standards on the basis of state sovereignty claims <p> Build a community of consensus on the importance of the rule-based international order of treaty compliance by all states <p> Invest in Canadian and international monitoring and regular reporting on China 's treaty compliance . <p> Through these measures and other efforts , Canada can help put relations with China on a more solid footing . Renewing Canada 's relationship with China in the wake of the Meng matter requires China to renew its commitment to compliance with its treaty obligations . <p> Pitman B.
